newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel hands over Hebron to PLO.
newsitem.headline: Israel hands over Hebron to PLO.

text.p: Israeli soldiers slipped from the headquarters of their 30-year-long occupation of Hebron at dawn on Friday handing over most of the powderkeg West Bank city to Palestinian rule.
Barely 100 Palestinians watched the pullback, the result of intense U.S. pressure on Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to save Middle East peace.

The soldiers drove down from the hilltop base only to set up a few hundred metres (yards) away. One fifth of the city will remain under Israeli control as protection for 400 militant Jewish settlers at its heart.

Hebronites said they were happy to see the back of the soldiers but worried because the Arafat-Netanyahu agreement left the settlers in enclaves around the Tomb of the Patriarchs, a site holy to Moslems and Jews.
The settlers called the pullback a betrayal. Led by a rabbi, some tore their shirts, a sign of mourning at the passing of Netanyahu's commitment to keep the biblical Land of Israel.

"At 6.10 the authority was turned over to the Palestinian Authority based on the Hebron agreement," said Israel's West Bank army commander, Major-General Gabi Ofir. "The keys were turned over successfully," he said.
One man climbed a 15-metre (50-foot)-high antenna atop the headquarters to raise the Palestinian flag over the building which Arafat was expected to visit within a few days.

Fireworks burst against the dawn sky but celebrations were muted for the long-delayed handover, the last of seven West Bank city transfers under an interim self-rule agreement between Israel and the PLO.
Palestinian Colonel Awni al-Natshe, deputy Hebron commander, said: "Today we will make the life in the city normal."
Blue-uniformed civilian police then fanned out to direct traffic and joint Israeli-Palestinian units began patrolling the border between Jewish and Arab areas.

"Now we must begin rebuilding the city," said Palestinian Mayor Mustafa al-Natsheh. He was confident the settlers would not cause trouble after the redeployment but few of his fellow residents were as sure.
"We want the settlers to go out of our city," said Hussein Awaiwi, 65, who lives near a market that has frequently been the scene of Arab-Jewish friction.
Israel poured troop and police reinforcements into Hebron to thwart settler protests.
"It's a sad day for justice," said settler spokesman Noam Arnon. "It's a victory for terrorists," he said referring to Arafat.
The Israeli army, however, issued orders restricting the movements of 18 alleged Jewish militants for up to 10 days to forestall trouble in a city scarred by Arab-Jewish violence.

The withdrawal accord, clinched after months of acrimonious negotiations, marked the first time a right-wing government had agreed to hand over territory Israel occupied in the 1967 Middle East war to PLO rule. It sparked a revolt in Netanyahu's coalition cabinet although it won overwhelming approval in parliament with opposition support.

Washington hailed the agreement as a building block for peace. But the foundations for future discord have already been laid with Israel and the PLO interpreting the deal's provision for three further West Bank withdrawals over the next 18 months differently.
